segments.en: Good to be with you.
I'm Tony Dokoupil.
The breaking news right now.
Was it radical indoctrination?

The Omani national who allegedly tried to hijack and crash that plane loaded with Israeli passengers may have terror ties, according to Israel's prime minister, investigators still searching for a motive.

Also tonight, outrage at Cornell, students holding a public hearing on the university's handling of that alleged frat gang rape, what the alleged victim did in the days after to document what she says happened.
Severe weather outbreak.
MAN 1: Structure just got hit.
TONY DOKOUPIL: Tornadoes, and flash flooding struck the central US, more than 100 million at risk tonight.
Christa is alive right now.
TONY DOKOUPIL: Failed execution-- a Tennessee woman now in critical condition after surviving two lethal injections meant to kill her, what went wrong?
The moment Florida deputies rescue a woman trapped in a burning car, what happened next.
And a race against time rescue in Oregon after a fisherman found himself pinned under a boulder, how he called for help.
Hey, guys.
TONY DOKOUPIL: And The Good Stuff, nothing but nets where they're needed most.
ANNOUNCER: From CBS News headquarters in New York, this is the CBS Evening News with Tony Dokoupil.
And good evening.
We begin tonight with the heroism on board that nearly doomed flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv on Wednesday, the co-pilot stabbing the captain and causing the plane to plummet toward the desert below.

But the wounded captain, seen here in new video, somehow managed to unlock the cockpit door, allowing a small group of passengers to push in, pull up on the controls, and then subdue the attacker using cords from a headset.
Our senior foreign correspondent Imtiaz Tyab reporting tonight from Tel Aviv.
IMTIAZ TYAB: On the cabin floor, Captain Smit Machchhar, the pilot hailed as a hero, can be heard asking for help.
SMIT MACHCHHAR: My head is spinning.
It's hurting.
IMTIAZ TYAB: The cell phone camera keeps rolling as Saudi first responders help the wounded Indian captain off the FlyDubai plane, the bloodied co-pilot accused of attacking him, seen on his knees.

Those chaotic scenes follow terror in the skies after the co-pilot, who CBS News has learned is of Omani origin, allegedly stabbed the captain inside the cockpit, with preliminary flight data indicating the plane then dropped 14,000 feet in less than 30 seconds.
Adam Polo was on board with his wife and children.
Was there ever a moment where you felt like you might not make it?
Absolutely.
Absolutely, of course.
It's terrifying.
And when you start to hear people scream, they're stabbing the-- we didn't know that there's replacement pilots on the plane.
MAN 2: You won't sleep.
IMTIAZ TYAB: Despite his wounds, Israeli officials say, Captain Machchhar managed to unlock the cockpit door.
One passenger says he briefly pulled back on the controls.
Then two reserve pilots traveling on board took over, safely landing in Tabuk, Saudi Arabia.
For families still in their seats, like Hila Evron, she told CBS Mornings, it felt like her time with her sons was near their last.
He just start to yell, Mom, I love you.
And that was the moment that I realized that my kid actually separating from me from the world.
IMTIAZ TYAB: But the crisis has raised huge questions about aviation security and how this could have happened.
Speaking to Fox News, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu suggested the attacker co-pilot had, quote, "Islamist radical indoctrination."
It looks like he had been radicalized.
I think it's too early to say whether he had any connections with Iran or with anyone else.
IMTIAZ TYAB: Captain Machchhar has since been airlifted to a hospital in the UAE, where Indian embassy officials say he's recovering well.
And the United Arab Emirates has launched an investigation into what happened on the FlyDubai flight that put 174 lives at risk, including whether there may be possible links to terrorism.
But the central question now is, how did a weapon enter the cockpit, and was it more than just luck as well as quick-thinking by passengers that prevented what could have been a deadly disaster?
Tony.
Imtiaz, thank you very much.
We also know more tonight about what happened in the days after a young woman says she was raped by multiple men at a Cornell University frat house, including how she documented the alleged attack.
Here's CBS's Tom Hanson.
TOM HANSON: CBS News has obtained copies of a number of documents related to the investigation into an alleged gang rape at a Cornell University frat house.
The former student says she felt, quote, "like bait.
I felt like lions around me.
It just was a totally debilitating place to be in."
She told campus investigators that she consumed ketamine that night, a drug that can leave users immobile, even incapacitated, and described the feeling as "lights are on, but nobody's home.
Your brain is not functioning at its proper level."

The Title IX report also revealed this statement from one of the accused male students, quote, "I was sorry that maybe if it wasn't consensual and she was victimized, I was sorry for not stopping it, just sorry that I felt like if something bad happened, I didn't stop it."

According to a transcript of her interview with campus investigators, she says she collected evidence, including the dress she wore that night and pictures of her bruises, and that two days after the alleged sexual assault, she went to a campus clinic to treat an infection.
Her attorney says she told doctors it was contracted in a traumatic way, and instead of being referred for a rape kit, she was advised to seek therapy.
Her internal processing went from denial to shame and ultimately, acceptance that she had been raped by people that she thought were her friends, he said.
Late this afternoon, a student organized town hall on sexual violence was held on campus.
I'm also speaking as a fellow Jane Doe.
TOM HANSON: Frustration and concern were on full display.
STUDENT: We need to hold each other accountable.
IMTIAZ TYAB: Among those attending Akshara Keshri, a Cornell junior.
I know plenty of women like Jane Doe who do feel unsafe at frat houses.
IMTIAZ TYAB: And have you talked to any of your girlfriends about this issue, and what are they saying?
They're saying the same thing.
They're just scared.
We're all scared.
We're more mad as well at the administration.
IMTIAZ TYAB: She says this is not just a Cornell problem.
But when women report issues to cops around the world, they are either not acted upon or simply ignored.
IMTIAZ TYAB: Do you think the onus should solely fall on women to keep each other safe?
No, it should not be "protect your daughter."
It should be "educate your son."
And I will die on this hill.
And, Tony, here's an alarming statistic.
A Cornell survey last year found more than a third of undergraduate women reported non-consensual sexual contact since entering school.
Now, the university declined our request for an interview.
We also reached out to all of the accused.
We heard back from lawyers for two, who denied the allegations, Tony.
Tom, thank you.
Thunderstorms are threatening the central US tonight following an outbreak of flash floods and tornadoes yesterday.
CBS's Jason Allen reports tonight from Fort Worth, Texas.
JASON ALLEN: Moisture from two powerful hurricanes in the Pacific rushed into the Southern and Central US.
The system spun up tornadoes in Kansas and flash floods in Texas and Nebraska, with rainfall rates in some areas reaching 4 inches per hour.
In Fort Worth, a bus plowed through city streets, flooding in heavy rain, while cars started to float.
Firefighters waded in to rescue a woman from her car and carried her to higher ground.
In Omaha, Nebraska, this truck fishtailed right in front of a car before sliding across several lanes of highway.
In Kansas, a tornado ripped apart this barn in a matter of seconds.
Here in Texas, the extreme weather comes after one of the longest dry streaks in Dallas and Fort Worth, 77 consecutive days without significant rainfall.
We just watched one of these big logs just rushed downstream, and it's blocking the drainage ways, along with a bunch of trash that is built up.
And that's causing all of these creeks, these rivers, to overflow, blocking some pretty major roads like this one.
The Texas Hill Country was also bracing for flooding, a reminder of the storms that caused deadly flash floods in July.
The house has been flooded twice so far.
Floods are evil and nasty, and you don't understand how disruptive they are.

Some cities in the Texas Hill Country have received more than 7 inches of rain in the last 24 hours, and there is still a flood watch that's in effect through tomorrow night, as all of that water starts to drain into streams and creeks.
Jason, thank you.
More storms are firing up tonight across the Southern Plains as well, and they are pushing east with more than 100 million Americans under a flood threat through the weekend.
Meteorologist Rob Marciano tracking it all, as always.
Rob, good evening.
Hey, Tony, this has become a really wide-reaching system all the way to the Great Lakes.

Chicago, you've been out of the rain for a couple of days now, and we do still have some flash-flood warnings that are in effect for Tyler, Texas, for San Antonio, although those have shifted a little bit to the east.
But all in all, this is a 1,300-plus mile stretch of moisture.
Houston, you're going to get it next.
And then we'll get another round of this as we go through tomorrow in some of the same areas.
So we'll get it redistributed into Little Rock and then down the I-10 corridor as well, a level 2 out of 4 as opposed to 3 out of 4, so slightly less tomorrow.
But still, that front was there.
It's going to hang around on top Gulf moisture, so anywhere from 2 to as much as 7 inches of rain into some of these areas.
And this will linger into the weekend.
Meanwhile, also in the weekend, Southern California into the heat, triple-digit stuff, near it, as you head towards Saturday and Sunday.
So summer not wanting to quit there as we head now into October.
Tony.
Rob, thank you.
We turn now to that failed execution in Tennessee.
Convicted killer Christa Pike said she was ready to die, ready to be free, as she put it, but instead, she somehow survived two doses of a supposedly lethal drug.
Here's CBS's Skyler Henry.
SKYLER HENRY: It was supposed to be routine, but the botched execution of Christa Pike has Tennessee officials now searching for answers.
There was no reason to expect it to not work.
But something didn't go well or right last night.
SKYLER HENRY: At 7:27 PM, Pike was seen by witnesses strapped to a gurney.
They watched as pentobarbital was administered.
Pike complained about pain in her arm.
At 8:05, the curtains were closed, but witnesses continued to hear her snoring, until they were ushered out at 8:53.
Pike has spent more than 30 years on death row for the 1995 gruesome murder of her classmate, Colleen Slemmer.
Pike's lawyers argued she should be spared because of untreated mental illness and severe childhood sexual abuse they say wasn't adequately presented to a sentencing jury.
Her lawyers now say she's in critical condition.
This is a completely unprecedented event.
Christa Pike is the only person we know of who survived the administration of lethal doses of injection drugs.

This is Tennessee's second failed execution attempt this year, and it comes just four years after an independent review exposed several repeated failures by the state to properly test those lethal injection drugs.
Tony.
Skyler, thank you.
President Trump today launched a campaign blitz for Republicans in the run up to the midterm elections, with some unexpected early stops in deep-red Oklahoma and Texas as well.
CBS's Nancy Cordes reports tonight from Denton, Texas.
But I can't get the word out.
NANCY CORDES: President Trump traveled here to Denton, Texas for two reasons.
The first was to promote his tariffs.
I'm really here for Ken.
NANCY CORDES: The second was to shore up support for Texas Senate candidate Ken Paxton, who told donors that Trump's last trip here didn't help, according to audio obtained by The New York Times.
KEN PAXTON: When we did that convention, it dropped our numbers.
Everybody's numbers dropped.
NANCY CORDES: This could help explain why, sky-high prices for gas and diesel that led Texas Governor Greg Abbott to declare a statewide disaster this week.
At least 15 states are offering some form of fuel tax relief as the war with Iran drags on.
And yet Trump claimed incorrectly today that "prices are way down from what Biden and the Dumocrats left us."
I give us an A+ on the government, on economics, on everything.
We're about-- NANCY CORDES: Trevor Theriot wouldn't go quite that far today, but he did say things are going well for him.
We're growing at 8%.
To me, that's success.
NANCY CORDES: Theriot owns a medical device manufacturing company here in Denton.
He says the research and development credits in Trump's Big Beautiful Bill helped him a lot and that tariffs have incentivized him to build more of his products here in the US.
I will say, 200% tariff would be impossible.
But the 10% to 25% that we've seen lately still dynamically works for our company.
President Trump, who just wrapped up here, has been considering a temporary ban on US diesel exports to help bring down fuel prices.
But there could be downsides, like the possibility of global price shocks.
And so for now, he's holding off, Tony.
Nancy, thank you.
We turn now to a rescue in Oregon in which Siri, that virtual assistant from Apple, helped save a man's life.
Carter Evans has our details.
And a warning, some of these images may be disturbing.
POLICE: I've located him.
CARTER EVANS: Look closely as the police drone video zooms in.
That's 28-year-old Joe Little pinned under a giant boulder.
A boulder started slipping.
He tried to catch himself.
He got thrown in the air, and it flew on top of him.
CARTER EVANS: Little's mom, Mindy, says he was trapped on a jetty where he was fishing alone in Hammond, Oregon Saturday, and the tide was rising.
He thought he was going to die.
CARTER EVANS: Police would have never even known to look for him.
But Siri saved the day.
He was wearing those behind-the-ear headphones, and he was able to say, "Siri, call 911."
CARTER EVANS: The drone eventually guided in rescuers, who freed him from the boulder.
A Coast Guard helicopter hoisted him to safety.
POLICE: Still the survivor aboard the aircraft.
CARTER EVANS: And flew him to the hospital, where he's recovering from a fractured skull and a broken jaw.
He just went fishing.
It's a miracle my son is alive.
CARTER EVANS: A remarkable rescue set in motion by Siri.
POLICE: Nice and slow.
CARTER EVANS: Carter Evans, CBS News.
Still ahead on the broadcast tonight, liftoff for NASA's new mission and the astronaut who will be up there in orbit during a milestone here on Earth.
TONY DOKOUPIL: Here's a look 260 miles above Earth, as the Dragon spacecraft has reached the International Space Station for a six-month stay.
It's got four astronauts on board, including one with another pretty big mission back on Earth.
CBS's Mark Strassmann has our story.
SPEAKER: Liftoff.
MARK STRASSMAN: Crew 13's six-month mission above Earth lifted off with zero complications-- well, one for Canadian astronaut, Josh Kutryk.
His wife, Heather, is due with their third child around Thanksgiving.
He'll be 260 miles off the planet.
Boy, girl?
JOSH KUTRYK: We don't know.
We like surprises.
Should be able to figure that out by now.
Will it be hard to miss the moment?
Of course.
But I think when we're older, we'll look back on it fondly because of the uniqueness and the excitement.
MARK STRASSMAN: Ask any husband.
The space station could have become Kutryk's doghouse.
But Heather Kutryk supports his childhood dream of space.
Not exactly a plan, but it's a great thing.
MARK STRASSMAN: Along with their children, Peter, he's seven, and Anna, she's five.
Maybe I'm delusional.
Maybe it'll hit me when he's actually gone.
But so far, I feel like we're going to be great.
MARK STRASSMAN: No one can promise him family leave in space, but NASA will connect the Kutryks virtually for the big moment.
We will definitely have to look at time off around that time frame, too.
We're going to have to talk about the parental leave part.
MARK STRASSMAN: Josh Kutryk's space mission is a shared family sacrifice.

It's exceptionally important, and I hope that my new child looks at it as such, as making some sacrifice, taking some risk, but doing so in the name of public service and the name, of my case, for Canada.
Over the decades, astronauts in space have missed the birth of a child three other times.
Tony, the family life they said goodbye to going up is very different than the one they say hello to coming back.
It sure is, Mark.
Thank you very much.
We're back with a close call rescue in Orange County, Florida.
Two sheriff's deputies rushed in to free a woman whose car caught fire after she hit a tree last week.
One doused the flames with a fire extinguisher.
The other checked on the driver, then both yanked her out on the count of 1, 2, pull.
Up next, The Good Stuff, a man working to improve his community one basketball court at a time.

We are back with The Good Stuff tonight, a story of a man who has made it his mission to make sure every basketball hoop in his community has a net on it, and he's not waiting around for someone else to hang it.
Just yesterday, in fact, Craig Campanella hung his 77th outdoor net of the year, well on his way to a goal of 100 basketball nets in 2026.
Hey, guys.
I want to put a net up there for you.
Can you give me 10 minutes?
Yeah, I got you.
TONY DOKOUPIL: He's been doing it after work and on weekends for months now, traveling around with a ladder and a spreadsheet of hoops in need, mostly around his neighborhood in Queens, New York.
And the local basketball players, they absolutely love it.
Because whenever I do it, they tell me how appreciative they are.
They say, oh my god, thank you so much.
And some of them cheer.
Yay!
It's so great.
TONY DOKOUPIL: But of all the problems of the world, why this one?
Well, for no other reason than that beautiful sound of a basketball falling through a net and the fact that Craig knows it makes people happy.
There are more important problems in the world, but this is something that I can do that is helpful and I enjoy doing.
So it's how I choose to give back.
After giving back on his own at $10.99 per net, Craig now says others are donating too, and he's got the perfect name for his little program, Nothing But Nets.
That's another day in America.
I'm Tony Dokoupil.
Thank you for watching.
For all of us here at CBS News, good night.
See you right back here tomorrow.
